source: Nafar, Venable, Kordjamshidi (2024) Reasoning over Uncertain Text by Generative LLMs (BLInD), Table 1 re-read in layout mode
finding: Closes the gap 4 table question. The GPT-4 few-shot chain-of-thought row is 78, 64, 36, 25, 22, 16, 7, 7, 7 for V2 to V10 (variables in the network). Zero-shot CoT is 79, 63, 27, 10, 17, 6, 5, 7, 6. So the earlier c10 numbers (78, 64, 36) were right. Plain answering without CoT is near zero for GPT-4 few-shot (3, 0, 1, 1, 2, 2, 1, 1, 0).
numbers: GPT-4 CoT zero-shot V2..V10: 79,63,27,10,17,6,5,7,6. CoT few-shot: 78,64,36,25,22,16,7,7,7. Basic QA few-shot: 3,0,1,1,2,2,1,1,0. 100 items per split; GPT-3.5, Llama3-70B and GPT-4 only (2024 models).
limits: Synthetic Bayesian networks written as text, not legal prose. Only 2024 models; no reasoning models (o1/o3, Claude thinking) tested, so the part of gap 4 about 2025-2026 reasoning models stays OPEN. Few-shot examples gave no gain beyond V4.
agent_relevance: Chain of thought alone collapses once the network has more than 3 to 4 variables. A legal evidence chain with 5+ linked items needs a solver, not just more thinking.

source: Nafar et al. (2024) BLInD, Table 2 (number extraction) and Table 4 (solver methods), same PDF
finding: Bearing on gap 5 (automatic offloading). When the LLM only had to copy the probabilities out of text, GPT-4 was exact on all of V2 to V10 (100 percent exact match of all numbers). Letting GPT-4 write a ProbLog program stayed at 96 to 100 percent. Writing plain Python (PAL with number extraction) fell from 99 to 10 percent. Monte Carlo code stayed at 88 to 100 percent. GPT-3.5 was worse (ProbLog 87 down to 35 percent; number extraction 100 down to 78).
limits: The context states every probability and every dependency explicitly, in a fixed style. So this tests translation of given numbers, NOT elicitation of hypotheses, priors or independence structure from messy case text. Gap 5 (priors elicited from text, wrong structure) stays OPEN. The Graph Generation table (Table 3) was not parsed from the garbled layout.
agent_relevance: Translation to a solver works well when the numbers and links are explicit. The hard, unmeasured step for a legal agent is deciding the hypothesis set and links in the first place.

source: Araya (2025) Do Chains-of-Thoughts of LLMs Suffer from Hallucinations, Cognitive Biases, or Phobias in Bayesian Reasoning?
finding: Closest thing found to gap 1. Three reasoning LLMs (Gemini Flash 2.0, o3-mini, DeepSeek R1) solved a base-rate puzzle (cat and pig clue story). With no hint they used only symbolic probability, never natural frequencies. When the prompt told them to use Gigerenzer's natural-frequency strategy they used it only partly: Gemini only relabelled the percentages and argued in words; o3-mini counted cases and got it right; DeepSeek R1 used a very long chain, reverted to percentages, and reached a wrong 50 percent in one run. The author calls this a 'phobia' of ecologically valid formats.
numbers: One problem family, 3 models, run once in Feb 2025 (Gemini twice). Reasoning length: o3-mini about 1,100 to 2,000 words; DeepSeek R1 about 5,500 to 8,500 words. No accuracy rates over many items.
limits: Qualitative, tiny sample, no equal-token comparison, no tool-computed baseline. Does NOT answer gap 1 (a perturbed-item benchmark with a convert-to-counts operator vs plain CoT); gap 1 stays OPEN. Author is an education researcher.
agent_relevance: Telling a model to use natural frequencies is not the same as getting it to do it. A scaffold step must force and check the count table (counts add up, N is stated), not just suggest it.

source: Li and Rui (2024) Dual Traits in Probabilistic Reasoning of LLMs, re-read: Table 1 and appendix
finding: Fifteen models, three experiments. On a base-rate task with a bland description, GPT-4o, GPT-4 and Llama-3-70B gave exactly the Bayes-correct posteriors (0.75 vs 0.25; odds ratio 9). With a stereotype-fitting description (computer scientist or humanities) the base rate barely mattered: posterior 0.78 vs 0.74 for GPT-4o, odds ratio about 1.25 instead of 9. The human average odds ratio there was about 2.0, so the models neglected base rates MORE than people did. Posteriors tracked similarity ratings (Pearson 0.90 to 0.98). Asked separately, GPT-4o gave priors of 2 to 4 percent, yet recalled 10 to 30 percent inside the judgment task.
numbers: Table 1 odds ratio, representative description (CS): gpt-4o 1.25, gpt-4 1.18, claude-3-opus 1.68, gemini-1.5-pro 2.58, mistral-large 1.62, llama-3-70b 1.52, humans 2.02. Uncharacteristic description: 9, 9, 8.86, 6.36, 3, 9; humans 2.25. Human values were read off a published figure by the authors.
limits: 2024 models. One task family (Jason/professor description). Prompts stressing Bayes' rule did not remove the effect for GPT-4o. Not a legal setting. Frontier 2025-2026 reasoning models were not tested here.
agent_relevance: Base-rate neglect appears when the evidence is vivid and descriptive, as in case narratives. Supply base rates as explicit numbers in a separate step and compute the posterior outside the model's judgment.

source: Koehler (1996) The base rate fallacy reconsidered: Descriptive, normative, and methodological challenges. Behavioral and Brain Sciences 19(1)
finding: Part of gap 7. Abstract read (full text paywalled). Koehler argues the claim that people ignore base rates is not supported: base rates are almost always used, more so when learned implicitly or given as frequencies, when reliable, and when more diagnostic than the individuating information. He also argues that mechanical Bayes labelling of errors is wrong when task assumptions are unchecked, and that real-world base rates are often ambiguous or unstable.
numbers: No numbers in the abstract. 17-page target article with open peer commentary.
limits: Only the abstract and publisher summary were read; the legal-relevant sections were not. A competing view to Kahneman-Tversky on neglect and partly to Gigerenzer-Hoffrage on format.
agent_relevance: Do not hard-code 'base rate neglect' as the only failure. The agent must first check that the reference class and base rate are reliable, which fits the G5 hypothesis and assumptions step.

source: Thompson and Schumann (1987) Interpretation of statistical evidence in criminal trials: the prosecutor's fallacy and the defense attorney's fallacy. Law and Human Behavior 11(3)
finding: Gap 7 stays OPEN for this paper. Only the bibliographic record was confirmed (Crossref: 54 references, Law and Human Behavior vol 11 issue 3). The Springer page redirects to a login wall and no open copy could be fetched. The experimental numbers (mock-juror samples and the share who committed each fallacy) were NOT verified.
limits: Do not quote any percentage for this study in the schema notes. Name only: it introduced the terms prosecutor's fallacy and defense attorney's fallacy.
agent_relevance: The defence attorney's fallacy (dismissing a match because many people share the trait) is a useful test case to add next to the prosecutor's fallacy.

source: Qiao, Cheung, Hampson, Lagnado (2026, ICAIL '26 preprint) Biased Judge: Recency Effects, Cautious Convictions, and Conservative Updating in GPT-4o's Legal Decisions
finding: Gap 6, partly closed for GPT-4o on a Sally-Clark-style vignette. Evidence order moved final guilt from 0.66 (defence then prosecution) to 0.40 (prosecution then defence). GPT-4o gave almost no Guilty verdicts when defence evidence came last (odds ratio 0.002). Judging step by step raised Guilty-verdict odds about 10.5-fold vs judging at the end. Framing as 'advising chatbot' gave the fewest convictions; 'mock juror' the most (odds ratio 7.49 vs advisor). Replicated on burglary and hit-and-run vignettes.
numbers: 960 trials on the murder vignette (956 analysed), temperature 0.7, GPT-4o only. Order effect F(1,994)=4645.65, partial eta squared 0.83. Response mode OR 10.55 [6.11, 19.12]. Role framing: legal expert OR 2.20, mock juror OR 7.49 vs advisor. Mean final guilt: step-by-step 0.55 vs end-of-sequence 0.51.
limits: One non-reasoning model (GPT-4o), 8 evidence items per side, text only, no adversarial exchange. Reasoning models not tested here. Preprint of an ICAIL 2026 paper.
agent_relevance: Order of evidence changes the verdict. A scaffold should re-run the evidence in more than one order, or accumulate log-odds item by item outside the model, and flag order sensitivity.

source: Qiao et al. (2026) Biased Judge, Bayesian comparison section
finding: Gap 6 on conservatism. When Bayes' rule was applied to the model's OWN elicited prior and likelihood ratios, GPT-4o's stated guilt probability moved in the right direction but too little: posteriors were lower than Bayes after prosecution evidence and higher after defence evidence. This held for all three role framings and both response modes. Authors suggest anchoring on its own earlier numbers and a next-token pull against large numeric jumps. The vignette is loosely based on Sally Clark.
numbers: Observed vs predicted probabilities differed significantly in stages 2 to 4 and 5 to 8 depending on order (exact t values only in the preprint figures). Humans in Qiao and Lagnado 2025 and Shengelia and Lagnado 2021 updated closer to Bayes.
limits: The Bayesian benchmark uses the model's own self-reported numbers, so inconsistency of those numbers is not separated from true under-updating. Single model.
agent_relevance: Keep evidence strengths as explicit likelihood ratios and let code multiply them. Do not accept the model's verbal 'new posterior' after each step.

source: Bessis, Wills, Wojciechowski, White, Pothos (2026) Legal Decision Biases in GPT: A Comparison with Human Judgment. Behavioral Sciences 16(3):437
finding: Gap 6: a newer model still shows the effect but weaker. Six simplified criminal cases, evidence order (guilt-first G-I vs innocence-first I-G) and single vs double rating. GPT-4o showed a clear recency effect (F(1,711)=424.76), with mean final guilt 4.24 (G-I) vs 6.04 (I-G) in the double-rating condition. GPT-5.2 showed the same direction but attenuated (4.75 vs 5.35; F(1,711)=71.24). Asking for an intermediate rating inflated GPT-4o's final guilt ratings (a 'measurement bias') but not GPT-5.2's.
numbers: 720 trials per model per prompt condition; the human original had 120 participants with 715 final judgments. Temperature 1 main run, 0.2 robustness (correlation across temperatures r=0.996 for GPT-4o, 0.989 for GPT-5.2).
limits: Simplified cases; reversing order also changes the story, as the authors note. Reasoning effort not varied. Only two OpenAI models.
agent_relevance: Newer models are less order-sensitive but not immune. Keep an order-permutation check as a cheap test in the agent.

source: Bessis et al. (2026) Legal Decision Biases in GPT, prompt engineering section
finding: Bearing on gap 8 (generic warnings vs specific steps). Three system-prompt variants (legal expert, meticulous, justify your answer) were tried against the baseline for both models, 720 trials each. The paper reports limited and inconsistent effects: none reliably removed order sensitivity or the evaluation bias. Generic carefulness or role prompts are weak.
numbers: 4 prompt conditions x 720 trials = 2,880 final ratings per model. Per-prompt effect sizes not recorded here.
limits: Not a Sally-Clark dependence task, and no explicit-hypothesis-listing prompt was tested. So whether listing competing hypotheses (G5) beats a generic warning on dependent-evidence tasks stays OPEN.
agent_relevance: Do not rely on 'be careful' wording. Test specific structure steps (list H1 and H2, state dependence) against it directly.

source: Divergent patterns of probabilistic reasoning in humans and GPT-5. Frontiers in Psychology (2026), run on the Huang et al. (2025) paradigm
finding: Gap 6 / joint-probability side of Sally Clark. GPT-5 (reasoning effort default medium, temperature 1.0) was run on 553 matched human participant profiles, 78 election probability judgments each. Humans had a conjunction fallacy in 58.5 percent of conjunction judgments; GPT-5 in 18.8 percent, almost all single fallacies (99.5 percent). Complementarity violations: GPT-5 near zero (marginal 0.00004) vs humans 0.248; joint 0.00108 vs 1.250. So GPT-5 is far more coherent than people but not perfectly coherent.
numbers: N=553 paired persona/human profiles; paired t(552) = -24.79 for conjunction fallacies, -24.53 for marginal complementarity, -44.74 for joint.
limits: Election forecast probabilities, not evidence weighing. Persona-conditioned prompts. No legal content. Coherence is not accuracy.
agent_relevance: Frontier reasoning models rarely break basic probability rules on explicit numbers. The remaining risk is conceptual (wrong hypotheses, wrong independence) rather than arithmetic.

source: An LLM canary in the online data coalmine: Bayesian reasoning problems as a capability-gap test for LLM contamination in online samples. Behavior Research Methods (2026)
finding: Indirect evidence for gap 3 (LLMs on Hoffrage-type problems). In two preregistered pilots (N=148) of a Bayesian training tool, 57 percent of Pilot 2 participants scored a perfect 5 of 5 on positive predictive value problems, versus a meta-analytic human ceiling of about 24 percent for one natural-frequency problem. The author reads this as LLM use by online respondents, implying LLMs solve such items far above human rates.
numbers: N=148; 57 percent perfect scores vs about 24 percent human ceiling.
limits: Abstract only was read; LLM use is inferred, not measured, and no DNA or legal items were tested. No direct LLM-vs-Hoffrage replication was found in any source searched.
agent_relevance: Textbook Bayes problems are no longer a hard test for frontier models; use perturbed, narrative and dependent-evidence versions to find real weaknesses.

source: Pompedda, Santtila et al. (2025) Evaluating firearm examiner testimony using LLMs: standard vs knowledge-enhanced systems. Journal of Psychology and AI 1(1)
finding: Gaps 2 and 10, partial. Only two university press releases were read (full paper blocked by access walls). LLMs replicated a human mock-juror study (Garrett et al. 2020) on firearm examiner testimony, memory reset between trials. Knowledge-enhanced models were more cautious and scientifically grounded; guilt and credibility ratings dropped when evidence was effectively cross-examined; unlike humans, the models did not convict on inconclusive evidence.
numbers: No figures available from the press pages. Models not named there.
limits: Second-hand summary. Does not test the prosecutor's fallacy or likelihood-ratio vs verbal format directly, so gap 10 (format sensitivity of LLM readers) stays OPEN.
agent_relevance: Adding forensic-science background knowledge to the context may make an LLM reader more cautious. Worth testing as a G5/G9 context step.

source: HelixCross (2026) Design and development of an AI-powered cross-examination simulation for forensic expert testimony training. Forensic Science International: Synergy
finding: Gap 2, related tool, no measurement. A prompt-engineered LLM agent with retrieval simulates defence cross-examination on a synthetic DNA case with embedded 'fallacy traps' and a ten-dimension coaching rubric. It targets likelihood-ratio interpretation, proposition discipline and activity-level overreach. Evaluation so far is informal developer testing, with no ratings or outcome data. A vendor-side model update broke session state.
limits: Abstract only. Alpha-stage. Says nothing on how often LLMs themselves commit the prosecutor's fallacy.
agent_relevance: Practitioners already expect LLMs to be used around LR wording. The listed traps (proposition discipline, activity level) could seed a test set.

source: Jackson, Andreadis, Ancker (2025) Large Language Models and Communication of Medical Probabilities. JAMA Network Open 8(12):e2550449
finding: Gap 9 side: how LLMs map probability words to numbers. Four chatbots (GPT-4o, Gemini 2.0, Grok 2, Claude 3.5 Sonnet), 800 prompts each. They often declined to give a number (abstention 93.5, 93.0, 76.1 and 30.9 percent). When forced, their numbers followed lay readings rather than European Commission guidance: for 'common' (EC range 1 to 10 percent) the models said 38.5, 65.5, 24.5 and 16.5 percent. Anxious wording and severity changed answers for 33 of 40 model-term pairs.
numbers: Abstention OR 3.25 for severity and 4.63 for anxious wording. 'Usual': humans 75.4 percent, LLMs 15 to 52 percent. 'Likely': 67 to 74 percent across models vs human 71.9.
limits: Medical adverse-event words, not forensic evidential terms. 2025 models without reasoning mode. No comparison with ground-truth Bayesian-network values, so the legal part of gap 9 stays OPEN.
agent_relevance: Verbal strength words are unstable across models and prompt tone. Force explicit likelihood ratios or ranges, and test each model for scale stability.

source: Large language models (LLMs) as jurors: Assessing the potential of LLMs in legal contexts. Law and Human Behavior (2025)
finding: Gap 2 / mock-juror comparison. Record-level summary only (full text paywalled): GPT-4o, Claude 3.5 Sonnet and o1 replicated a mock-jury experiment. They were more consistent than humans but not bias-free: higher mean guilt probabilities but fewer convictions, racial bias, sensitivity to the number of allegations, and unlike humans higher guilt for shorter reporting delay.
limits: Seen only through a database abstract summary. Not about probability format or the prosecutor's fallacy.
agent_relevance: Guilt probability and verdict threshold are separate quantities in LLMs too; track both.

source: Cuellar (2025) The Prosecutor's Fallacy and Expert Testimony: A Modern Take Using Likelihood Ratios (arXiv 2502.03217)
finding: Context for gap 2. Abstract read. Argues experts and lawyers must present evidence so as to avoid the prosecutor's fallacy, that experts should report likelihood ratios not posterior probabilities, and that lay people struggle with LRs. Illustrated with a modified real case. No LLM content.
agent_relevance: Supports a rule that the agent states what it can and cannot say: it reports an LR for the evidence and leaves the posterior to explicit priors.

source: Analytic Misjudgment of Drug Safety Evidence and Causality: From the Prosecutor's Fallacy and Simpson's Paradox to Artificial Intelligence. Drug Safety (2026)
finding: Narrative review (abstract read) naming misread conditional probabilities and missing denominators as recurrent errors in drug-safety causality, and warning that AI tools without transparency may amplify them.
limits: Review with selected case studies; no LLM measurement.
agent_relevance: Shows the prosecutor's fallacy as a general conditional-probability error outside law; the same check (state both conditionals) can be reused.

source: Search log for gaps 1, 2, 3, 10 (what was NOT found)
finding: Searches of Europe PMC (including preprints) and arXiv title and abstract queries found no study that (a) measured how often an LLM commits the prosecutor's fallacy on realistic forensic prose, (b) re-ran the Hoffrage 2000 DNA problem with LLMs or with legal professionals in 2020-2026, (c) tested a natural-frequency rewrite operator on a frontier model at equal tokens with many items, or (d) tested LLM readers on forensic conclusion format. Several arXiv, Semantic Scholar and OpenAlex queries were rate-limited, so absence is not proven.
limits: Web search budget was exhausted by parallel agents; Semantic Scholar and OpenAlex returned 429. Treat as 'not found', not 'does not exist'.
agent_relevance: These four are open experiments for our own harness, not literature to cite.
